proposals.name: THE LEDGER
proposals.one_line: The market kept books for 180 years; this is those books, kept in public — every chart is a column of figures you can still read, and every figure says how sure it is.
proposals.philosophy:
The governing idea is that a table and a chart are the same encoding at two different speeds, and that this project needs both at once.

Cleveland and McGill rank position-along-a-common-scale as the most accurately decoded visual channel. A ruled column of right-aligned tabular figures IS position along a common scale — with an exact label attached. The difference between a column and a bar chart is not kind but precision-versus-speed: the column is exact, slow and unbounded in resolution; the bar is approximate, preattentive and bounded. So "charts emerge from tables" is not a decorative conceit. It is a literal, continuous, reversible transformation between a symbolic representation and a spatial one, and performing it in front of the reader — with the numerals never moving — teaches that the bar IS the number. That is the strongest available defence against the reader treating the picture and its source as two separate objects, which is exactly the failure mode a 505-claim calibrated dataset cannot afford.

The second argument is about where uncertainty lives. Chart idioms have no native slot for epistemic status. They have position, length, hue, area, texture — all of which are already spoken for by the data. So every chart-first direction must either spend a data channel on confidence or bolt on a legend the reader must hold in working memory. A document idiom arrives with four empty, pre-built slots that cost zero data-ink in Tufte's sense: the column rule, the footnote, the margin, and the stamp. Grade, interval, basis, as-of date and source all have a home that was already on the page. This is the single strongest reason to choose THE LEDGER over any alternative for this specific dataset.

The third argument is about absence. A ledger has a legible, honest, native representation for a number that does not exist: a ruled cell left blank. No chart form has this. A line that stops is ambiguous (did the quantity go to zero, or did the counting stop?); a ruled empty cell is unambiguous — the row exists, the period exists, nothing was entered. Given that this project's most important fifteen years (2011–2025 by medium) have no free series at all, and that era 1 has no annual series whatsoever, the ability to draw nothing legibly is not a nicety. It is a requirement.

Finally, coherence in Mayer's sense. Archival visual language is usually delivered as texture — sepia, stains, torn edges, drop shadows, photographs of documents. All of that is extraneous processing: it competes for the same limited channel the data needs, and it triggers a "historical, therefore inert" frame on a story whose last third is about 2026. THE LEDGER is therefore typographic, never photographic. The document is asserted entirely by structure and type — ruling, tabular figures, hanging indents, small-cap column heads, footnote apparatus, stamps. Not one pixel of simulated paper grain.
proposals.why_this_project:
Four reasons that are specific to this material and would not transfer to a generic data story.

**1. The subject of all four threads is a document.** Who counted (an audit certificate), who took a cut (an invoice), who was allowed in (an application form), who owned the door (a payment authorisation). A chart-first direction has to *represent* these institutions with colour swatches on a timeline. THE LEDGER can show the instrument itself. Thread 3's A-grade exhibit — Overture's entry gates against AdWords' in the same year — is not a quantity at all; it is a form with five fields, filled in twice. The highest-fidelity encoding of that evidence is the form.

**2. Heavy uncertainty needs somewhere to live that is not the chart.** 505 claims, three grades, 80% intervals on everything, 65 of them too wide to be points, 19 concordance entries, 32 cross-checks with 6 flagged, 28 bridged points all grade C, one declared taxonomy seam and one unranked triple. That is a catalogue problem before it is a chart problem, and catalogues are what archives solve. The margin, the footnote and the stamp absorb the entire rigor layer without touching the data ink.

**3. The two hardest problems have exact accounting idioms and no chart idiom.** Era 5's twin taxonomies are a *restatement* — in accounting you do not overwrite the old books when a classification rule changes; you publish the period twice on both bases with a reconciling line between them. That is precisely what the frozen record does. And era 7's three mutually unranked pools are an *unruled block* — in a ledger, ruled rows are ordered and an unbracketed set is not. Both problems dissolve into existing paperwork conventions. No chart form supplies either.

**4. The evidence itself is paper.** Coen's workbook, the 1919 Census of Manufactures Table 12, the FY2004 10-K's delivery contingency, Overture's 10-K benchmarking itself against Yellow Pages calls, the Mehta findings of fact. Showing the paperwork is not a metaphor laid over the research; it is citation made visible. The gap between $255.6m of census receipts and a $1,200m benchmark for the same year 1914 is not a discrepancy to be smoothed — it is two different forms, filled in by two different parties, for two different purposes, and the ledger form is what makes that legible instead of embarrassing.

hard_problems.solution:
THE FOLIO — four registered views on one shared time ruler, plus one governing rule printed on screen: "One sheet, one ruler. Two rulers means two rows."

**View 1, THE SPINE (always present).** Total US advertising as two ribbons that are never joined. The encoding is taken from the invoice itself: the billings basis (Coen/McCann, 1919–2007, what advertisers were charged) is drawn as the GROSS RAIL with its hairline above the ribbon; the media-owner revenue basis (MAGNA, 1980–2025, what sellers received) is drawn as the NET RAIL with its hairline below. The vertical distance between the two rails in the 1980–2007 overlap is not a problem to hide — it is the intermediary's cut, made visible, which means P1's seam and thread 2 become the same object. Where only one rail exists, the other is drawn as a dashed hairline in `--unassigned` at the bridge's estimate, inside a hatched band at the bridge's own interval, never as a solid line. The chapter-09 restatement (2007: $279.6bn billings against about $230.9bn media-owner, a 17.4% level difference) is therefore something the reader sees as the height of the wedge rather than something they must remember.

At 1980, a **wedge card** sits in the margin: a 100% micro-bar decomposing the 23.4% gap into 69% category scope and 7.2 points price basis, carrying its own 60–78% range and a note that it rests on one overlap year.

**View 2, THE COMPOSITION SHEET.** By medium. Explicitly not a stacked area or streamgraph. Instead a small-multiple ledger: one 34px row per medium, all sharing the identical time ruler and an identical 0–40%-of-total y-scale, each row a filled area from its own zero baseline, with the medium name in an Archivo small-caps stub column at left and 1919 / 1949 / 1975 / 2007 values in tabular figure columns at right. Rows sort by peak year, so the "new media enter small and take decades" finding becomes a visible diagonal. Nine rows show by default (every medium that ever exceeded 3%), grouped 3/3/3 by heavier rules; `SHOW ALL 27` expands to the full label set. Where a series stops, the row's cells are ruled and blank. The 2011–2025 by-medium hole (`ds-gap-001`) is a visibly empty ruled block with one stamp: `NO FREE SERIES · 2011–2025`.

**View 3, THE MONEY-TYPE SHEET.** See P5 for its unranked-safe form.

**View 4, THE CROSS-CHECK COLUMN.** A persistent 120px right-hand column that, for the currently scrolled year, lists which of the eight series are live, their values, the cross-check verdict, and any concordance note. It is generated from `Object.keys(adspend.series)` with a build-time assertion that fails if fewer than eight keys render — the structural answer to Gate A's "do not hard-code five series keys." The 1999 Billboards-to-Out-of-Home change (2.77× on identical data) surfaces here as a concordance note, not as a 177% jump.

Data-to-viz caveat gate: the two-ribbon line passes (two lines, uncut y-axis, direct labels, no dual axis). Small multiples are data-to-viz's own prescribed remedy for stacked-area's unreadable middle bands. Streamgraph, stacked area, pie and dual-axis are excluded by rule across the whole project.
hard_problems.cognitive_rationale:
Stacked bands force the reader to judge band *thickness* — length without a common baseline — which sits near the bottom of the Cleveland–McGill accuracy ranking, and the error is worst exactly for the middle bands that carry this story. Aligned small multiples upgrade every comparison the reader actually needs (which medium is biggest, when did each peak, which crossed which) to position along a common scale, the top of the ranking.

Sharing one x-ruler pixel-for-pixel across all four views turns the time axis into a single learned chunk rather than four re-reads, which is a direct working-memory saving under a 4±1 constraint that is already strained by seven eras and eight fields.

The two-rail treatment is the Tufte principle that a difference in the data should appear as a difference on the page. A footnote saying "different basis" must be held in memory and will not be; a visible vertical gap between two rails is external cognition and cannot be forgotten. And the blank ruled cell exploits Gestalt closure in reverse: a ruled row with nothing in it is perceived as an unfilled slot, not as a zero.

hard_problems.solution:
ERA 1 IS NOT ON THE SPINE — IT IS A TIPPED-IN PLATE, AND THE JOIN IS A PHYSICAL GUTTER.

**The plate.** 1840s–1917 gets its own page object: narrower than the main sheet, set on `--desk` rather than `--stock` so it reads as a different stock of paper, and ruled in *decades* rather than years. The seven benchmark years appear as ledger entries, not points. Each is a right-aligned tabular figure with its 80% range printed beneath it in old-style figures in the same cell, plus a horizontal range rule whose length is the interval on a shared log money scale: 1867 $50m (30–80), 1880 $200m (140–280), 1890 $360m (260–480), 1900 $495m (400–600), 1909 $1,070m (880–1,270), 1914 $1,200m (990–1,450), 1917 $1,500m (1,250–1,800). Both estimate lineages are shown as two rules per year where they differ — the 1914 pair at $1,100m and $1,302m sit as two rules, not as an average.

**The gutter.** At 1918/1919 there is an actual 28px vertical band of `--desk` running the full height of the chart, stamped vertically in Archivo small caps: `DIFFERENT BASIS`. Nothing is ever drawn across it. Not a line, not an annotation, not a hover. The pre-1919 totals are a promotional-outlay measure of which print was only about 21%; the post-1919 series is a media measure. The gutter says so structurally.

**Era 1's timeline is documents, not money.** Because era 1 has no series but exceptional institutional detail, its scroll runs on artifacts rather than years, and this is where the whole reading grammar is taught: Palmer's claim of 1,300 of 2,000 papers (drawn as a range rule, 700–1,400, because it is an agency selling itself); the Sun's one-cent front page; the 1875 open contract; the 1893 recognition rule that made 15% enforceable; a Rowell directory page; the 1912 sworn circulation statement; and the 1914 ABC certificate with its three funders named. Each is a typographic reconstruction in the project's own form language — a ruled form with the real figures in it — never a photograph.

So era 1 occupies eight scroll scenes while contributing seven data points, and it is experienced as *the era of paper without numbers*. It is the reason the rest of the experience is a ledger.

**The GDP trap** is handled by the gutter too: 3.3% in 1914 and 3.0% in 1922 sit on opposite sides of it, with one marginal note in `--pencil`: "Two rebuilds. Not one line."
hard_problems.cognitive_rationale:
Uniform connectedness is the strongest grouping cue in the Gestalt inventory — stronger than proximity, colour or similarity. Breaking connectedness with an unfilled band is therefore the strongest possible "these are not one thing" signal available, and it needs no legend and survives every colour-vision condition, every screenshot and every print. A dashed segment, by contrast, still reads as one line with a stylistic variation, which is exactly the phantom-continuity failure the brief warns about.

Changing the *unit of the axis* rather than the scale solves the pixel-allocation problem honestly. Seventy-seven years cannot be given half the horizontal ruler when it has seven observations, but it can be given eight scenes when it has eight artifacts. The reader's sense of duration comes from scroll distance, not from axis width, so era 1 feels like half the story without any chart claiming annual resolution it does not have.

Teaching the grammar on the era with the *worst* numbers is deliberate sequencing: the reader meets the range rule, the hatch, the old-style figure and the stamp when nothing else is competing for attention, and arrives at the auction already fluent.

hard_problems.solution:
REPLACE JITTER WITH RULING. The primary uncertainty encoding is static, and jitter is demoted to a single licensed quotation.

**The four-part grammar.**

1. **The range rule.** Every calibrated quantity is drawn as a hairline spanning its 80% interval, with the central marked by a heavier *tick* — a ruler's mark — never a dot. A dot asserts a point; a tick marks a reading on a scale.
2. **The suppression rule, enforced in code.** `if (ciWidth / central > 0.6) suppressCentralTick()`. The 65 claims above that threshold are drawn as a span with no central mark at all. This is not stylistic; it is a build assertion. Its most striking consequence is that era 1's entire 1914 money-type row loses every tick — national brand 11–46%, local retail 15–46%, direct response 8–30%, classified 1.1–5%, unassigned 5–55% — so the reader sees five spans and not one point, which is exactly what "only one ordering is safe: classified was smallest" looks like. Era 7's row, by contrast, shows two ticks (national brand, direct response) and two spans (local retail, classified), and that visible difference is itself information.
3. **Grade as hatch pitch.** The band behind each rule is A = solid `--wash`; B = 45° hatch at 6px pitch; C = 45° hatch at 3px pitch. Texture density is a preattentive channel fully separable from position and hue, so it never competes with the value, and it survives greyscale, colour blindness and print.
4. **Figure set as provenance.** Source Serif 4's lining figures for filed or audited numbers; old-style figures — which visibly rise and fall against the baseline — for our own estimates. Purely reinforcing, never load-bearing alone; the hatch and an appended small-cap A/B/C always carry it too.

**The audit stamp.** Every chart carries its own grade mix in the lower right (`A 12 · B 31 · C 4`), and the project header carries `A 133 · B 260 · C 112`. Clicking any stamp opens the claim ledger filtered to that chart. Rigor becomes a countable object rather than a mood.

**Why replace jitter, in three arguments.** (a) Motion is the most involuntarily attention-capturing preattentive channel there is. In P1, where uncertainty *was* the thesis, spending the loudest channel on it was right. Here the thesis is institutional power, and the loudest channel must be reserved for narrative transitions. Five hundred shimmering marks would leave no attentional budget for the argument. (b) Jitter cannot express the two uncertainty shapes this project most needs: "two intervals overlap so neither is larger" and "a residual nobody can allocate." A vibrating point still asserts a point. A span with no tick does not. (c) A static primary means reduced-motion readers, print readers and screenshot readers get the identical encoding, not a fallback.

**The one licensed quotation.** In thread 1's 1987 people-meter exhibit, the *instrument* is the subject, so the audience figure jitters within its interval while the instrument toggle is mid-flight, then locks. Scope declared, borrowed from P1 by name, used once.
hard_problems.cognitive_rationale:
Garner and Ware's separability criterion: position carries value, texture density carries confidence, figure set carries provenance, and none of the three interferes with reading the others. Hue is left entirely free for the semantic that actually matters here — who did the counting.

Suppressing the central tick is a Norman mapping argument. The affordance of a dot is "this is where it is." When the interval is wider than 60% of the central, that affordance is a lie the design is telling on the data's behalf. Removing the mark removes the lie, and because the rule is mechanical, it cannot be quietly overridden by an author who likes a cleaner chart.

The stamp addresses the availability heuristic. Readers estimate reliability from what comes to mind, and what comes to mind is whichever number was most vivid. A visible per-chart grade count anchors reliability to a count rather than to vividness — the same reason a footnote apparatus works better than a disclaimer.

hard_problems.solution:
THE RESTATEMENT — a two-column sheet with a reconciling column and a hinge.

When an accounting classification changes, you do not overwrite the books. You publish the same period twice, on both bases, with a reconciling line between them. That is what the frozen record does, so that is what the sheet does.

**Layout.** Left column head, Archivo small caps: `ERA-NATIVE BASIS — SPLIT BY ADVERTISER GEOGRAPHY`. Right column head: `CROSS-ERA BASIS — ONE INTENT POOL`. Between them, a 64px reconciling column containing exactly one row: `LOCAL YELLOW PAGES, 2000 · $11,135m · 4.50 POINTS`, with a hairline arrow from the left column's local-retail cell to the right column's direct-response cell.

Both columns show all four pools as range rules with their intervals. Under both rules, local retail and direct response visibly overlap. Left: 28.32 against 24.71. Right: 23.82 against 29.21. A `--pencil` marginal note sits under both: "Under both rules these two overlap. Neither is bigger."

**The hinge.** A two-position toggle labelled `BASIS`. Never a slider — a slider implies intermediate positions that do not exist, and the control's form must map to the state space. Flipping it animates *only* the $11,135m block, which travels between columns as a single object over 500ms (the FILE verb), while every other figure stays pinned and visibly unchanged. Their cells get a 1px `--rule` outline during the transition to prove they did not move. The reader watches one block move and two orderings swap.

**The stamp.** Whichever ordering is currently displayed receives a stamp reading `ARTIFACT OF CLASSIFICATION`. The stamp lands on the *ordering row*, not on the data — a deliberate placement, because the data are not in question and the ordering is.

**The caption**, at the readability gates: "One block of money moved between two pools. The market did not move at all. Nothing written at the time says which pool it belongs in."

Cross-era enforcement: any chart that places era 5 beside another era is hard-wired to the unified-intent basis and shows a small-caps basis chip in its header. The geographic basis is available only inside era 5's own chapter. Splicing them crosses an undocumented redefinition worth 4.4995 points of the 2000 market, and the code will not do it.
hard_problems.cognitive_rationale:
This is a change-blindness problem before it is anything else. If the whole sheet re-renders on the toggle, the reader cannot tell what changed — Rensink's result is that a single altered element in a re-presented scene is very often missed, even when it is large and central. Pinning every other cell and moving exactly one block converts a re-render into a tracked motion, which the visual system handles preattentively and effortlessly.

This is the user's object-constancy preference doing genuine epistemic work rather than decorative work. The same $11.1bn keeps its identity across two taxonomies. Because it is the *only* thing with a changed identity, the reader's unavoidable inference is that the taxonomy moved and the money did not — which is the exact claim, delivered by perception rather than by prose.

Showing both columns simultaneously rather than sequentially converts a recall task into a recognition task. A toggle that replaces one view with another requires the reader to hold the previous ordering in working memory to detect the swap; two columns side by side put both orderings in the visual field, where comparison is free.

hard_problems.solution:
THE UNRULED BLOCK — a brace, no row rules, no row numbers, and a brace that shuffles when you touch it.

No stack, no bar chart, no ranked list. Era 7's four pools are drawn as four range rules on one horizontal share-of-market scale (0–50%), arranged vertically, and the arrangement is structurally marked as non-informative.

**The brace.** The three mutually unranked pools — national brand, local retail, direct response — are enclosed by a printed brace in `--unassigned` spanning their rows, labelled once in Archivo small caps: `ALPHABETICAL · ORDER NOT ESTABLISHED`. Alphabetical is a recognisably non-informative ordering, which is why it is chosen over any data-derived order.

**The missing rules.** Inside the brace there are no horizontal row rules and no row numbers. Everywhere else in the entire experience, ruled rows are numbered and ordered. This is a structural convention that costs one legend on first appearance and nothing thereafter: ruled means ordered, unruled means a set.

**Classified sits outside and below the brace**, with a full rule above it and a row number, because its ordering against the other three *is* established. So the sheet shows a set of three and one ranked item — which is precisely the state of the evidence.

**The overlap is drawn.** Where two range rules share x-territory, the shared span is filled `--wash` and hatched. Tap or hover gives: "These two share this range. Neither is bigger." National brand's 25–47 and direct response's 29.5–47 overlap across most of their length, and the reader sees why the 1.4-point gap between their centrals means nothing.

**The interaction.** Touching the brace re-shuffles the three enclosed rows once, with a 320ms move. Nothing else changes: no figure, no rule length, no overlap. The gesture teaches unrankedness kinetically — the reader learns that the vertical order carries no information by watching it not matter. A passive reader is never disoriented, because the shuffle only fires on deliberate contact.

The same block form is reused for era 1's five 1914 pools (all five unranked except that classified is smallest) and for era 7's brand-versus-response pair in chapter 09. Learned once, used three times.
hard_problems.cognitive_rationale:
A stacked bar commits two separate integrity offences here. It forces a length-without-common-baseline judgement, near the bottom of the Cleveland–McGill ranking, and it asserts a total order the evidence explicitly refuses. Four aligned range rules on a common scale give the correct judgement — position on a common scale — while asserting nothing about order.

The brace works because enclosure creates a common region, which is the strongest Gestalt grouping cue and, critically, the only one that groups *without* implying sequence. Proximity, similarity and continuity all leave a reading order intact; a brace does not.

Removing the row rules removes the sequence affordance in Norman's sense. Ruling is what makes a list a list. An unruled cluster does not invite the eye to read down it in order, which means the reader is not silently constructing a ranking the design then has to argue against.

And the shuffle is enactive learning. A caption saying "these cannot be ordered" is a proposition the reader must accept on authority. A shuffle that visibly changes nothing is a demonstration, and demonstrations survive in memory better than assertions.

hard_problems.solution:
THE COMPARATOR — the simulator is not a page of the ledger. It is the desk the ledger sits on, and on that desk there is an adding machine.

This is the direction's load-bearing test, so the metaphor is made to do real constraint work rather than decorative work.

**Three zones, fixed for all 21 scenarios.**

1. **THE RATE CARD (left, 30%).** Inputs as a form. Three advertiser rows (Aster / Brindle / Cedar) with editable bid, predicted CTR and true CTR fields — predicted and true always in visibly separate columns with a heavier rule between them, because keeping those two arrays apart is the model's single most important structural decision. Above them the rules block: `RANK BY: bid | bid × click rate`, `PAY: next bid + $0.01 | your own bid`, the reserve field, and the three-position `BIDDER MODE` toggle. Every field carries a provenance mark in small caps: `INVENTED` in `--unassigned` on the cast, `FILED` in `--auditor` on disclosed figures, `ASSUMED` in `--seller` on gamma.

2. **THE TAPE (centre, 30%).** An adding-machine tape running downward in IBM Plex Mono, printing the arithmetic line by line as the auction resolves: AdRank per bidder, rank, price computed, clicks, revenue. One tape line = one arithmetic step, and the steps that print are the machine-checkable steps in `mechanism.json`. When an input changes, the tape **reprints from the changed line downward** and every line above stays pinned — so the reader sees exactly which steps the change touched. This is only possible because the metaphor is a tape, and it is the single best teaching device in the whole design.

3. **THE STATEMENT (right, 40%).** Revenue per 1,000 impressions, total clicks, average price per click, each with its delta against the previous run in `--redink` or `--auditor`. Permanently below it, **the band strip**: a ruled horizontal scale from $440 to $760 with a tick at the current bidder mode, headed `GSP REVENUE IS A BAND · 1.727×`. Every revenue figure printed anywhere on the desk carries the current bidder mode as a superscript. A revenue number without a bidder mode is never rendered.

**The metaphor enforces the build constraints.** The distribution engine (D1–D11) is a *different sheet*, reached by a page turn, because the auction engine's invented per-1,000-impression figures must never share an axis with filed dollars. Physically different sheets means physically different axes; the category error the build notes warn about becomes structurally impossible rather than merely discouraged. Similarly, sc-10 is rendered as **two facing pages** — display recto, search verso — with arrows running in opposite directions, because facing pages is a ledger's native form for "compare two things" and it makes "opposite directions" a spatial fact rather than a sentence.

**Guards against teaching a dead mechanism.** Every sheet carries `AS AT: 2008` or `AS AT: 2019` in the same header position, so the date is checkable rather than readable. sc-06 carries its caption as a printed footer rule, always visible and not dismissible: "This was display. Search never went to first price." The pay-your-bid comparison row is printed under a `FROZEN-BID COUNTERFACTUAL` stamp, with the 86% apparent windfall from Google's own 10-K example labelled as what it is. `take_rate_syndicated` appears with a permanent `AUCTION OUTCOME, NOT A LEVER` label and the 9 → 24.7 → 21.5 → 21.3 series printed beside it. `advertiser_pool_elasticity` renders only as a two-position toggle stamped `UNMEASURED`, never as a continuous control.

**Scroll order in chapter 07:** sc-01 → sc-02 (the sign reversal: revenue +86.6%, clicks +222%, price per click −42%) → sc-03 → sc-04 → sc-05 (the band) → sc-07 (breakeven true CTR 1.99%; overstatement up to 2.5×) → sc-08 (one bidder, $0.40 against $40.00, 100×) → sc-09 (the knobs) → sc-06 → sc-10.

**TAKE THE PEN.** At any point the reader can seize the controls. Their run is stamped `READER'S RUN — NOT A SOURCED SCENARIO`, and when they scroll on it FILEs into the left margin as a tape stub they can reopen. This is the proof the archive is alive: the reader's own experiments become entries in it.
hard_problems.cognitive_rationale:
Mayer's segmenting principle is why 21 scenarios are one-per-scroll-beat and reader-paced rather than a control panel: a panel with 21 configurations exceeds working memory instantly, while a docket of 21 entries is a sequence of single comparisons.

Spatial contiguity is why the tape is between the inputs and the outputs rather than below the fold. The split-attention effect is severe for arithmetic: if the numbers that produced a result are elsewhere on the page, the reader must carry them, and they will not.

The reprint-from-the-changed-line behaviour is signalling in Mayer's sense, implemented as motion onset — the only lines that move are the lines that changed, so attention is directed by the data rather than by the designer.

The fixed three-zone frame across all 21 scenarios reduces visual search to near zero after the first one. This is the standard consistency argument, but it matters more than usual here because the scenarios differ in *which* variable is live, and a stable frame means the reader's only search task is "what is highlighted," not "where is anything."

And the band strip is an anchoring defence. Any single revenue figure will be anchored on. A permanently visible band with the current position ticked on it makes the anchor a *range*, which is the honest object.

hard_problems.solution:
THE ERA PLATE, THE TRANSPOSE, AND THE CONSPECTUS — the same eight fields, two orientations, one fold-out.

**The plate (per era, identical seven times).** Each era chapter opens on a ruled eight-row form in fixed order: CREATORS / BUYERS / SELLERS / MEDIUM / SCALE / PRICING / MEASUREMENT / TARGETING. Header block carries era number, years, name, and the mechanism sentence. Each row is one line of about twelve words plus one figure with its range rule. Because it is the same form seven times, byte for byte, the reader learns the row positions and can read any era's PRICING row without reading its label.

Eight rows exceeds working-memory capacity, so the plate is chunked into three blocks separated by a heavier rule: **WHO** (creators, buyers, sellers), **WHAT** (medium, scale), **HOW** (pricing, measurement, targeting). Three chunks of 3 / 2 / 3.

**The ninth field is deliberately not on the plate.** Events are temporal, the other eight are structural, so events live on the time ruler as stamped dates. The split is stated once, because an unexplained 8-row form against a 9-field schema is a discrepancy a careful reader will notice.

**The transpose — the answer to "without scrolling twice."** Every row label on every plate is a control. Click it and the sheet unfolds horizontally: that one field becomes a seven-column strip, one column per era, all seven visible at once on desktop (7 × 150px = 1,050px). The rest of the page dims to `--desk`. So a reader in era 6 who wants era 3's PRICING does not scroll at all — they transpose. This is the ledger's native operation, and it is the single most useful navigational affordance in the project.

Each transposed strip carries its own comparability warning where one is needed. Thread 2's hole applies here: the PRICING strip's seven columns do not share a denominator, so each column header prints its own denominator in small caps, and columns on a genuinely different basis are set on `--desk` rather than `--stock`. Different paper means different form.

**The Conspectus.** A standalone sheet reachable from the contents: all 56 cells at once, about nine words each, ruled, with the three block dividers and the seven era columns. At 13px this fits one desktop screen. It is the reference artifact the archive would actually contain, and it is where a returning reader starts.

**The plate is also the era's index.** Each cell's figure is a live link into the claim ledger, so the plate doubles as a table of contents for the era's evidence.
hard_problems.cognitive_rationale:
A repeating identical form is Tufte's small-multiple argument applied to text. Holding position constant means the only variance the eye detects is content, so a reader flicking between two era plates perceives *difference* directly rather than reconstructing it by reading. This is the difference between comparison as perception and comparison as reasoning, and it is roughly an order of magnitude in effort.

The transpose is a direct working-memory intervention. Comparing era 3's pricing to era 6's in a linear document requires holding one cell across roughly eight thousand words, which is simply not possible — the comparison will not be made, and the schema's whole point will be lost. Putting both in the visual field simultaneously moves the comparison from memory to perception, which is the only place it can actually happen.

The 3/2/3 chunking follows the standard capacity result: eight undifferentiated rows will be read as an unstructured list and retained poorly; three labelled groups are retained as three items, each of which unpacks on demand.

And the plate supports recognition over recall throughout. A reader never has to remember what the eight fields are, because the form shows them every time, in the same order, in the same place.

hard_problems.solution:
A LEDGER IS ALREADY A SINGLE VERTICAL COLUMN. That is this direction's largest structural advantage and it should be claimed plainly: on mobile, the other directions degrade, and this one arrives at its native form.

**No sticky hero stage.** The SPINE pins as a 132px strip at the top — two ribbons only, no medium detail, with the current scroll year ticked. It is a running header, not a stage, and it is capped at under 20% of viewport height so reading area never drops below 60%. Prose scrolls beneath it.

**Charts become tables again, and nothing is lost.** Below 640px the composition sheet renders as its stub column plus three figure columns (1919 / 1975 / 2007) with a 60px inline sparkline per row — an actual table, scrolled vertically. This is not a fallback; it is the source. In a chart-first direction the mobile version is a compromise. Here it is the original document.

**The transpose becomes a swipe.** One era per snap-scrolling card, field name pinned at top, seven cards. The Conspectus becomes a two-axis scroller with a frozen stub column.

**The simulator reduces to the tape plus toggles.** The reduction is unusually cheap here, because the frozen spec already insists that every pedagogically load-bearing control be a toggle rather than a slider — `bidder_mode`, `query_denominator_path`, `partner_delivers`, `advertiser_pool_elasticity`, `nontac_cost_allocation`, `ranking_rule`, `pricing_rule` are all discrete by design. All of them survive at 48px hit targets.

Continuous variables are replaced by their own marked stops as two- or three-button steppers: gamma gets `1.0 | 0.50` (which is the stop where squashing restores the pure-bid allocation while collecting 45% more than pure bid ever did), reserve gets `$0.01 | $1.00`, format multiplier gets `1.000 | 1.075`, shading factor gets `0.60 | 0.667 | 0.733`. The scenario file supplies every one of these stops already.

The tape prints in a four-line window with a `SHOW ALL STEPS` expander.

**Deliberately dropped on mobile, stated plainly:** free numeric entry on the rate card; drag-a-bid on sc-04; the continuous gamma, format-multiplier and terminal-multiple sliders; D1's cumulative-revenue slider; D5's rpm drag; the four-view Folio seen simultaneously; the wedge card's fine decomposition (it becomes a tappable footnote); and PULL THE RULE as a drag (it becomes a tap-to-toggle on the column head).

**What survives, and it is the argument:** sc-02's sign reversal, sc-05's band, sc-07's misestimation, sc-08's reserve, sc-10's two directions, the BASIS hinge, the unranked brace, all seven era plates, all four thread visuals and the entire claim ledger are fully reachable on a phone using toggles and steppers alone.

**Rendering adjustments.** Hatch pitch doubles (6→8px, 3→5px) because fine hatch aliases badly at 375px on high-DPI. Grade also appends a small-caps letter to every figure, since texture is less reliable at that size. The SPINE strip is Canvas; everything else stays DOM and SVG because an archive's text must be selectable and findable. Particle counts cap at 2,000, with a static fallback under 360px.

**The honest summary:** on a phone the reader gets the argument and the evidence. They do not get the sandbox.
hard_problems.cognitive_rationale:
The split-attention effect is the governing constraint on mobile: a sticky chart plus scrolling prose forces the reader to integrate two spatially separated sources through a viewport too small to hold both. Capping the pinned strip at 132px and making it a header rather than a stage keeps the integration cost near zero, because a header is glanced at, not read.

The toggle-over-slider preference is Norman's mapping principle and it happens to coincide exactly with touch ergonomics. A slider implies a continuum of meaningful positions; almost every important control in this simulator has two or three meaningful positions and the rest are noise. Converting them to steppers on mobile therefore loses no information and gains thumb-reachability — a case where the accessibility fix and the honesty fix are the same fix.

And the table-as-fallback is the coherence principle at work. Removing the graphical layer removes decoration, not content, because in this design the graphical layer was always derived from the figures rather than substituted for them.

hard_problems.solution:
FOUR VISUALS, THREE OF WHICH REUSE DEVICES ALREADY TAUGHT.

**Thread 1 — THE AUDIT REGISTER.** I argue against the two-track timeline and for a register. Keep both quantities but change the layout: one row per counting institution, in founding order, each row carrying the institution name in the stub, a `PAID BY` column, a funding bar segmented by funder, and a span rule for its years of operation on the shared time ruler. ABC 1914, CAB 1930, Hooper 1934, Nielsen 1950, BRC 1964, people meters 1987, DART 1996, FAST 1998, the seller's own log 2002, Analytics 2005, MRC/Nielsen 2021.

The reveal is the `PAID BY` column read vertically: advertiser · advertiser and publisher · rival medium · vendor · industry · industry · … and then, from 1996 down, SELLER · SELLER · SELLER · SELLER. A column of repeated identical tokens pops out preattentively; a colour-coded ribbon does not. Behind the register runs a vertical `--auditor` band spanning 1914–1996, ending abruptly with a stamp: `RULE BROKEN`.

Two inset exhibits. **1987**: a two-position toggle, `INSTRUMENT: household meter | people meter`, with the measured prime-time audience falling 10% and CBS and ABC each 13%, and the rate-card figure visibly re-typing beneath. This is the one place P1's jitter is retained — the audience number vibrates while the instrument is in flight, then locks. **2021**: one stamped line, `UNDERCOUNT 2–6% · VALUED AT ≥ $468M`.

**Thread 2 — THE SEVEN INVOICES.** Seven invoice forms, one per era, identical layout, one declared convention printed in each header (share of the advertiser's gross outlay). Line items: agency, network or publisher rep, seller platform, exchange, media owner. Figures right-aligned; PULL THE RULE turns each figure column into bars. Each invoice header prints its own denominator in small caps, so the reader can see that the seven denominators differ, and invoices on a genuinely different basis sit on `--desk` rather than `--stock`.

Era 7's invoice **cannot be totalled**. The ISBA 15% unattributable delta is a hatched line item labelled `UNATTRIBUTED`, the total line prints as `———`, and a stamp reads `DOES NOT BALANCE`. An invoice that will not balance is the entire thread in one image, and only a document direction can produce that object.

**Thread 3 — TWO SHEETS THAT DO NOT JOIN, AND ONE FORM BETWEEN THEM.** Left sheet: the classified and directory dollar share, eras 1–4, as range rules on a 0–15% scale. Right sheet: advertiser head count, eras 5–7, on a labelled log rule — 3,800 → 53,000 → 80,000 → about 1M (drawn as a span with no central tick, since 550k–2.6M is 2.05× the central) → over 10M. Between them, the same 28px `--desk` gutter used at 1918, stamped `DIFFERENT MEASURE`. The reuse is the point: the reader learned this device in era 1.

Between the sheets, **the GATE CARD** — one form, two columns, 2002:
```
                 OVERTURE      ADWORDS
MINIMUM BID      10¢           none
MONTHLY MINIMUM  $20.00        none
REVIEW           by hand       automatic
ACTIVATION       —             $5.00 once
```
Tapping either column stamps a specimen application `ACCEPTED` or `RETURNED`. Small, memorable, and it dramatises an A-grade finding without inventing a number.

**Thread 4 — THE STANDING ORDER.** One recurring payment-authorisation form, reproduced seven times, only the payee and the amounts changing: subsidised third-class post; the affiliate station at 27% of network net time sales (Mutual at 3.5%); the station rep at 5–20%; USPS again at $9,817m in FY1993; Overture's affiliates at 56%; AOL at ~85% plus a warrant; Apple at $20bn in 2022 on a 36% Safari rate, against $26.3bn of all default payments in 2021.

Two separate figure columns, never a dual axis — the rate as a share of the revenue it generated, and the absolute dollars on their own log rule. Dual-axis charts are excluded across the project because the crossing point is arbitrary and therefore rhetorical. Two columns say the same thing without the trick, and the thread's point is exactly that the rate barely moved while the money grew about 40 times.

The AOL warrant inset: two figures on one row, `AT SIGNATURE $13,871,000` and `REALISED $1,134,643,000`, with a rule between and a note — "Same paper. Eighty-two times the money." The closing stamp on the 2025 form: `EXCLUSIVITY BARRED · PAYMENT PRESERVED`.
hard_problems.cognitive_rationale:
All four are small multiples of an identical form, which is the canonical encoding for "same operation, different parameters." Holding the form constant makes the varying cell the only signal, which is maximal signalling at zero additional ink.

Thread 1's change from two tracks to a register is a binding-cost argument. A two-track timeline asks the reader to bind a top element to a bottom element by vertical adjacency across a long horizontal axis — a demanding conjunction search that gets harder as the axis lengthens. Moving the funder into an aligned text column converts the finding into repeated identical tokens in a single column, which is a texture the eye detects without search. The most devastating thing about this thread is a word appearing four times in a row, and words in a column are the right encoding for that.

Thread 2's unbalanceable invoice is a Gestalt closure violation deployed on purpose. The reader has seen six invoices close. The seventh does not, and the discomfort of an unclosed form is the argument.

Thread 3's reuse of the gutter is amortised learning: an expensive convention taught once in era 1 pays off three more times, so the reader's total vocabulary stays small even as the number of visuals grows.
