palette.role: The sheet. Ground for every live page, table, chart and form. Warm book stock, not simulated paper texture.
The surface behind the sheet. Page background, the 28px basis gutters, forms on a different basis, dimmed states during a transpose. A different colour of paper means a different form.
Ink. Body prose and every tabular figure. Iron-gall warm black, ~15:1 on stock.
Hairlines. Column rules, row rules, axes, sheet edges, the brace. 1px at all sizes; never thicker, never coloured.
An independent count. Third-party audit bodies, filed and verified figures, the credit side, the 1914–1996 discipline band. Half of the workhorse colourblind-safe pair.
The interested party's own number. Seller-computed metrics, the intermediary's take, assumed parameters. The other half of the workhorse pair; use #7E4F0C for text below 14px.
Corrections, losses, impairments, foreclosure, DOES NOT BALANCE, and all stamps. A ledger column semantic, used often — a deliberate divergence from P1's single-use red.
Residuals and refusals. Era 1's 37.8% unassigned, era 7's unranked brace, ISBA's unattributable 15%, bridged estimates, nobody-counted. The colour of an honest hole.
The auditor's hand. Marginalia in the gutter, secondary text, captions, provenance notes. Set in italic at 0.85em, never a handwriting face.
Confidence-interval band fill, hatch ground, shaded overlap regions, era bands, the 1980–2007 wedge.

proposals.type:
Three faces, each with a job, and one typographic device that carries provenance for free.

**Source Serif 4 (variable) — the sheet.** Body prose AND every figure, in the same family. This is the ledger's central typographic claim: numbers live inside the document, not on top of it, so prose and tables share one voice. Chosen over alternatives because it definitively ships all four figure sets plus small caps. Column figures run `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums lining-nums`, which is what makes a column of digits vertically alignable and therefore scannable as a scale. Display sizes use the optical-size axis at low weight (76px/0.95, weight 300) so titles read as a printed head rather than a web hero.

**The figure-set device.** Lining figures for a filed or audited number; old-style figures — which visibly rise and fall against the baseline — for our own estimate. It costs nothing, adds no ink, and gives an entire dataset a texture that separates measured from constructed at a glance. It is always reinforcing, never load-bearing: the hatch pitch and an appended small-caps A/B/C carry the same information redundantly, because font-feature support is the first thing to fail under fallback.

**Archivo (variable, including the width axis) — the chrome.** Column heads, form labels, legends, era plate headers, stamps, basis chips. Always uppercase or small caps, letterspaced 0.06–0.10em, 10–12px. This is the visual language of an accounting form, and it is the only sans on the page. Archivo Narrow is used where a seven-column transpose gets tight. Stamps use Archivo at weight 700 with a single shared SVG ink-bleed filter (feTurbulence into feDisplacementMap, baseFrequency 0.9, scale 0.8) — one filter, at most six stamps on screen, and disabled entirely under reduced motion.

**IBM Plex Mono — the machine.** The simulator's tape, live readouts, arithmetic derivations, claim IDs. This is a deliberate semantic split: the archive is set in the book face, and the adding machine on the desk prints in the machine face. The reader can tell at a glance whether a number is a record or a computation. Carried over from P1's data chrome, which makes it the one face the repo-wide review will not have to argue about.

**Rejected: handwriting faces of any kind.** Marginalia are set in Source Serif 4 Italic in `--pencil`. A script face would be kitsch, would fail at 15px, and would signal "olde tyme" on a story that ends in 2026.

All three faces are variable, subset to Latin plus the required figure sets, and preloaded — static GitHub Pages, and FOUT on a page whose whole argument is typographic would be fatal.
proposals.motion:
Six named verbs. Everything on screen moves in exactly one of them, or does not move.

**POST — 220ms, cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.25,1).** A figure enters its cell. Digits roll up from the least significant position and lock right-aligned; the cell's underline draws left to right over the final 80ms. Used for every value arriving in a table, and for every line the simulator tape prints.

**RULE — 400ms, linear (~1,400px/s).** A hairline draws along its length. Axes, column rules, era bands opening, the discipline band behind the audit register. This is P1's SWEEP renamed and re-scoped: near-linear, because a ruling pen moves at constant speed.

**TALLY — 600ms, cubic-bezier(.16,1,.3,1).** The table-to-chart morph, and the system's most-used verb. A cell's baseline rule extends out of the table into a bar or line. The rule and the bar are the same DOM element; the numerals never move. This curve is P1's SETTLE, adopted deliberately and by name.

**STAMP — 140ms in, 90ms settle.** Grade marks, audit stamps, ARTIFACT OF CLASSIFICATION, DOES NOT BALANCE, RULE BROKEN. Arrives at 1.06 scale with 0.4° rotation, lands at 1.0, with a 3px ink-bloom (a blurred duplicate at 12% opacity, fading over 400ms). Maximum one stamp animating at a time. This is the only organic motion in the system, and it is what makes the archive feel handled rather than printed.

**FILE — 500ms.** A row or block leaves the live sheet and docks into the margin as a 4px condensed stub. Used for retiring scenes, for the reader's own simulator runs, and — critically — for the single $11,135m block travelling between taxonomies in the BASIS hinge.

**ANNOTATE — 300ms fade plus 8px rise.** Marginalia entering the gutter in `--pencil` italic. Never simultaneous with any other verb; one change at a time, always.

**Uncertainty does not move.** This is the deliberate break from P1. The primary encoding is a static ruled span, static hatch pitch and a static figure set. Measurement jitter survives in exactly one exhibit — the 1987 instrument toggle in thread 1, where the instrument is the subject — and is declared as a scoped quotation.

**prefers-reduced-motion.** POST: figures present at final value, underline drawn instantly. RULE: instant. TALLY: 200ms cross-fade between table and chart states, shared element holding position. STAMP: present at 1.0, no rotation, no bloom, filter disabled. FILE: instant dock. ANNOTATE: instant. The BASIS hinge and the brace shuffle both become instant swaps with a 1.2s `--wash` highlight on the elements that changed, so the "what moved" information survives without motion.

The important property: because the entire rigor layer is static by design, a reduced-motion reader loses narrative polish and loses nothing epistemic. There is no fallback encoding for uncertainty, because there was never a motion encoding to fall back from.
proposals.signature_interaction:
**PULL THE RULE.**

Any figure column anywhere in the experience can be grabbed at its right edge and pulled. Dragging right extends each cell's baseline rule outward into a bar proportional to its value. Dragging back retracts it into the table. The numerals never move: they stay in their cells, right-aligned, at their original positions, for the entire gesture. Release snaps to fully out or fully in over 600ms on the TALLY curve.

Mechanically: a 12px hit strip in the column's right gutter, marked with a faint `⇥`; `pointermove` maps 0–160px of travel onto 0–100% of bar length; keyboard users focus the column head and use left and right arrows. Every column ships with an authored default state, so the reader is never required to discover it in order to read the page — they discover it, once, because a bar they are looking at retracts under their cursor.

Why this is the one the reader remembers. It is the philosophy performed as a gesture: the reader physically converts a symbolic representation into a spatial one and back, and sees that nothing was created or destroyed — a rule was extended. It is available everywhere, so it is learned once and used a hundred times. It hands the reader control over their own encoding preference, which is a genuine accessibility win: a reader who wants exact values keeps the table, a reader who wants shape pulls the rule, and neither is second-class. And it is object constancy in its strictest possible form, with a single persistent element carrying identity across the two representations.

Its most dramatic deployment is on era 7's money-type sheet. Pull the rule there and the four bars extend — and three of them visibly overlap, inside a brace, with no rules between them. Touch the brace and the three rows shuffle; the overlaps do not change. In one gesture and one touch, the reader has drawn the chart themselves and discovered that three of its four quantities cannot be ordered.
proposals.what_it_sacrifices:
**1. Spectacle, and the screenshot contest.** There is no full-bleed particle field, no dark mode, no cinematic opener. Against a particle-first direction this loses the first-impression comparison decisively. P1's beat 1 — 160 shimmering marks — is more arresting than three ruled rows, and it always will be.

**2. The particle metaphor is genuinely weakened.** The user's standing preference is one particle equalling one real unit, morphing across scenes. THE LEDGER preserves object constancy strictly, but its carrier is a row and a rule, not a free-floating unit, and true particle fields survive in only two places (the 1987 audience exhibit, the AOL warrant inset). If the attachment to particle scrollytelling is strong, this direction under-delivers it, and no amount of arguing about Cleveland–McGill changes that.

**3. Density is a cliff.** Ledgers reward slow reading. The payload here is in figure columns, so a skimmer gets substantially less than they would from an annotated-chart direction where the shape carries the headline. The thirty-second visitor leaves with the least of any direction on the table.

**4. Historicism fights the last three chapters.** "Archival" can read as "old," and this story's hottest argument is about 2019–2026. The form is most native to eras 1–4 and least native to era 7. Mitigations exist — the adding machine on the desk, the register rather than a scrapbook, no photographic texture anywhere — but the tension is real and chapters 08 to 10 will have to work against their own container.

**5. The rigor grammar leans on fragile channels.** Figure sets and hatch pitch are excellent on a calibrated desktop and degrade on low-DPI screens, at small sizes, and under font fallback. The redundant small-caps letter grade is mandatory everywhere, which adds label clutter that a colour-first uncertainty system would avoid.

**6. Build cost in text rendering.** A real archive means selectable, findable DOM and SVG text rather than Canvas. That caps particle counts, makes the largest sheets heavier, and forces virtualisation on the Conspectus (56 cells) and the composition sheet (27 medium rows across 107 years). A Canvas-only direction would be materially faster.

**7. It is worst at exactly what a streamgraph is best at.** Smooth, felt, continuous change over 107 years is deliberately given up. Small multiples are the correct encoding and they are less visceral. A reader will leave THE LEDGER knowing precisely when each medium peaked and will not have felt the century flow past them. That is a real loss and it is the price of the middle-band readability the brief demands.

**8. The typographic discipline is a single point of failure.** The direction refuses paper texture, refuses handwriting, refuses photographs. If the build cannot hold that line — if one stakeholder wants a scanned rate card — the whole thing collapses into pastiche, because the argument is that the document is asserted by structure alone.
proposals.first_screen:
Viewport 1440×900, no scroll.

Full-bleed `--desk` #E6E0D2. Centred on it, a sheet of `--stock` #F7F4EC, 1040px wide, running off the bottom edge of the viewport. 1px `--rule` on the right edge, a 2px #D8D1C0 edge on the left so it reads as a bound gutter. No drop shadow — a ledger page is bound, not floating.

**Header block**, at the top of the sheet, in the exact form every era plate will later use, so the grammar is taught in the first second. Left, Archivo small caps, 11px, letterspaced 0.08em, `--pencil`: `UNITED STATES · ADVERTISING · 1840 — 2026`. Right, same style, two lines: `AS AT 30 JUNE 2026` and `A 133 · B 260 · C 112`. A 1px `--rule` under the block, full sheet width.

**Title**, Source Serif 4, weight 300, 76px/0.95, `--iron`, ranged left:
> The Attention Economy

Beneath it, 22px Source Serif 4 Italic, `--pencil`, 46ch measure:
> *One hundred and eighty years of putting a price on a stranger's attention.*

**Then the hook, which is three ledger entries.** A four-column ruled block, hairlines above and below, taught before anything else exists:

```
1867      $50m          ├──────────────┤ (3px hatch, no central tick)    ESTIMATE
1914      $1,200m       ├────┤          (6px hatch, no central tick)     ESTIMATE
2025      $405,000m     ├─┬─┤           (solid wash, heavy tick)         FILED
```

Money column right-aligned in tabular lining figures for 2025 and tabular old-style figures for 1867 and 1914. Range rules on a shared log money scale. Fourth column Archivo small caps, `--pencil`. Three rows, and the entire rigor grammar is taught with no legend and no instruction: wide and scratchy means unsure, a heavy tick means filed, and a number with no tick has no point value at all.

**Margin note**, out on the `--desk` to the right of those rows, `--pencil` italic 15px:
> *Every number here says how sure it is.*

**Bottom edge**, cropped by the fold: the top 40px of the SPINE — two ribbons beginning, with the 28px `DIFFERENT BASIS` gutter at 1918 already visible as a vertical band. The crop is the entire scroll affordance. Bottom-left of the sheet, `BEGIN` in Archivo small caps 12px with a `⌄`.

No navigation bar, no logo, no hero image, no button, no cookie banner.

**Motion on load.** Nothing for 300ms — the sheet is simply there. Then the three entries POST at 120ms stagger: 1867, 1914, 2025, each figure rolling into place with its underline drawing behind it. At 900ms the `A 133 · B 260 · C 112` stamp lands with its 0.4° rotation and ink-bloom. Total 1,040ms, then stillness. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` everything is present at 0ms.

**What the reader knows after five seconds:** this is an archive; it covers 1840 to 2026; it is about money; every figure declares its own confidence; there is a chart below and it is already broken into two pieces.
proposals.divergence_from_p1:
P1's language is provisional and the repo-wide system settles at a later combined review. Here is the precise list that review must reconcile.

**1. One ground becomes two.** P1: bone #F2EEE4 with a 22px grid. P2: stock #F7F4EC on desk #E6E0D2, with the sheet as a discrete object. The review must decide whether the repo has one paper or a paper-on-surface system. I would argue for the latter, because the second ground is what makes the basis gutters and the different-form convention possible at zero legend cost, and P1 could adopt it without changing anything it already ships.

**2. The workhorse pair keeps its axis and changes its meaning — the sharpest item.** P1: amber #E0972A = PRICE, cyan #3AA6BD = COST. P2: seller #A96C14 = the interested party's own number, auditor #2F5D7C = an independent count. Both are orange-against-blue, both colourblind-safe, both single-purpose within their project — and they are different semantics on the same axis. The review has two choices: declare a repo-level abstraction that both instantiate (something like "the interested reading against the disinterested reading," which genuinely covers price/cost and seller/auditor), or keep local semantics and require a per-project legend at the hub. I favour the abstraction, because if the hub cannot state one meaning for its own primary colour axis, it is not a system.

**3. Red stops being single-use.** P1 reserved #C6432B for capital risk only, hatched and labelled. P2 makes #B3372B a column semantic used dozens of times — corrections, losses, impairments, stamps, does-not-balance. These cannot both be house rules. The review must pick: rare accent, or ledger-red convention. If it picks rare accent, P2 loses its most natural mapping and must find another colour for the debit column.

**4. Uncertainty: kinetic primary versus static primary.** P1 makes measurement jitter the core device everywhere. P2 demotes it to one scoped exhibit and makes the primary a static ruled span plus hatch pitch plus figure set. I would argue the review should adopt static-primary with kinetic as a licensed special case, on three grounds: it survives reduced motion, print and screenshots identically; it can express overlap and unrankedness, which jitter cannot; and it frees the motion channel for narrative. But this is a real reversal of P1's central claim and should be argued, not assumed.

**5. Motion verbs.** P1: SETTLE, SWEEP. P2: POST, RULE, TALLY, STAMP, FILE, ANNOTATE. TALLY explicitly reuses SETTLE's curve; RULE is SWEEP re-scoped. The right resolution is probably two shared *curves* (critically-damped arrival at cubic-bezier(.16,1,.3,1); near-linear draw) with project-local verb names, because a verb is a semantic and the semantics genuinely differ. Forcing one vocabulary across projects would flatten meaning to save a glossary.

**6. Type is the deepest disagreement.** P1: Martian Mono numerals as heroes, Newsreader prose, IBM Plex Mono chrome — the thesis being that numbers are the protagonists. P2: Source Serif 4 for prose *and* figures, Archivo chrome, IBM Plex Mono for the machine — the thesis being that numbers live inside the document. Only Plex Mono survives both, and only for machine output. These are opposed positions about what a number is, and they cannot both be the house rule. The review will have to choose, and whichever it chooses, one project's central typographic argument becomes a local exception.

**7. Unit metaphor.** P1: one particle equals one calibrated unit, morphing across scenes. P2: one row or rule equals one entry, with true particle fields scoped to two exhibits. The hub needs an explicit statement on whether object constancy in this repo is carried by particles specifically or by any persistent element. I would argue the latter — the principle is identity across transformation, and a rule that becomes a bar satisfies it as strictly as a dot that moves.

**8. No conflict on mode.** Both are light-only. Both refuse a dark default.

proposals.name: The Bench
proposals.one_line: One bench, seven machines: learn the apparatus once in 1840, and you can operate every era after it — including the auction.
proposals.philosophy:
The reader's problem with 180 years of institutional history is not that the facts are hard. It is that seven eras times eight fields is 56 things to hold, and visual working memory holds about four. Every choice in this direction spends its budget buying SPATIAL CONSTANCY instead of memory.

The apparatus is a single machine drawing — the bench — with eight organs at eight fixed screen positions, redrawn seven times. INLET (buyers), GATE (who is allowed in), METER (measurement), RULE (pricing), SORTER (targeting), DOOR (who owns the attention), TOLL (the intermediary's cut), OUTLET (sellers), with SCALE as a dial and EVENTS as a strip beneath. Once that layout is learned, comparing era 3's pricing to era 6's stops being a recall task — serial, slow, error-prone across saccades — and becomes a position judgment, which is parallel, preattentive, and Cleveland & McGill rank 1. The schema is not a table. It is a floor plan.

Interaction follows the same logic. There is exactly one verb, CRANK: set the input, turn the handle, read the output. It is learned in era 1 and reused six times. Hick's law then works for us instead of against us — the choice set never grows, only what sits inside the box changes. This is why seven operable mechanisms is affordable: the cost is front-loaded into chapter 2 and amortized across the rest. By era 6 the reader has cranked five machines and knows precisely what the handle does, which is exactly the fluency the auction simulator needs and cannot build for itself.

And the machine frame does something no chart frame can. A mechanism drawing already expects tolerances, hatch, stated limits and "not to scale" notes. So 505 calibrated claims with 80% intervals, three source grades, 19 definitional seams and one documented fifteen-year hole sit INSIDE the metaphor rather than fighting it. A chart apologizes for its error bars. A machine drawing specifies them.

The four threads are not extra chapters bolted on. They are the four organs that persist while the rule changes: the METER, the TOLL, the GATE, the DOOR. Each thread chapter is one organ pulled out of all seven benches and lined up. That is the structural claim: who counts, who takes a cut, who is let in, and who owns the door are the four parts of a price machine that are not the price rule — which is exactly why they are the parts that carry the power.
proposals.why_this_project:
Because the four selected threads are literally organs of a mechanism, not quantities. "Who counted, and who paid the counter" is a meter and its funder. "The intermediary's cut" is a valve on the outlet. "Who was allowed to buy" is a gate on the inlet. "The rent on the front door" is a door. No other frame makes those four things one object; under a "quantities rise and fall" frame they are four unrelated essays. The bench is the only structure I can find under which the threads are cross-sections rather than digressions — which matters because Gate B explicitly chose them for being about institutions and power rather than about totals.

It also fits the specific epistemics. This project's uncertainty is mostly NOT sampling noise. It is definitional: a 23.4% gap in 1980 between two compilers measuring different objects, a Billboards-to-Out-of-Home line that jumps 2.77x on identical data, an era-5 taxonomy where the classification rule decides which pool is larger, three era-7 pools that cannot be ordered at all, and fifteen years with no free by-medium series. A machine drawing handles definitional uncertainty natively, because engineering drawings routinely carry two dimensions for the same feature under two conventions, plus a note. A line chart does not have that vocabulary; it can only draw a line and then apologize in a caption, and the line wins.

And the story's shape is mechanical. Chapter 7's finding is that quality weighting raised total revenue while cutting price per click 42% — a result nobody believes from prose and everybody believes after turning the handle themselves. Chapter 7 also establishes that GSP revenue is a band, not a number, which is a statement about a machine under-determining its own output. That is not illustrable. It is only operable.

hard_problems.solution:
A five-component chart SYSTEM with a fixed grammar, reused everywhere. (1) RAILS — one per compiler, each a physically distinct material on a shared 1840-2026 time axis. coen_mce (1919-2007, billings) is a solid ribbon whose thickness IS its 80% CI. magna_mg8 (1980-2025, media-owner revenue) is a second solid ribbon, different hue, crisper edge. iab_pwc is a narrow inlaid rail. irs_soi is DOTTED, because a tax deduction is not a media market. naa_newspaper appears only on the classified axis. All eight series keys are loaded; none is hard-coded away. (2) CALIPERS — at the 1980 overlap the two ribbons are drawn with a visible parallax gap and a labelled measuring caliper between them reading '23.4% — same year, same country, two rulers.' The caliper body is itself DECOMPOSED into a wide hatched segment (69% category scope) and a thin segment (7.2 points price basis). (3) PINS — census_manufactures grade-A receipts drawn as small hard-edged filled squares that puncture the ribbons; the only official independent aggregate before 1960 gets the highest-salience mark form. (4) BRIDGE — bridge_mce_mg8 is never a continuing line. It is a hatched vertical offset girder with its own interval, drawn between the ribbons. (5) At 2007 the Coen ribbon ends in a hard RAGGED CUT EDGE, labelled 'Coen stops here. No successor on this basis.' The Magna ribbon continues alone, and the reader already knows why it sits lower, because the caliper explained it 27 years earlier on the same screen. No phantom collapse, because the collapse was pre-measured.

BY-MEDIUM: never a stack, never a streamgraph. The LANE BOARD — 11-14 horizontal lanes, one per medium, each 34px tall, each drawing its share from its OWN common baseline, all lanes sharing one x-axis and one y-scale. Lanes sorted by peak year, so the diagonal cascade of 'each medium's moment' is itself the finding: newspapers read as a 73-year plateau, radio as a lane that never gets tall. A lane goes hatched and splits into two disconnected bands at a definitional change (Billboards/Out of Home at 2000). Post-2010 every lane except internet goes to grey STIPPLE with one label: 'No free by-medium series exists after 2010.'
hard_problems.cognitive_rationale:
The phantom-collapse failure is a Gestalt GOOD-CONTINUATION error: the eye welds two aligned segments into one line and reads the offset as an event. Annotation cannot fix this, because the percept forms before the caption is read and picture-superiority means the percept wins. Only three things break continuation — different material, a physical gap, and an explicit connector object — so the system uses all three at once. Placing the caliper at 1980 rather than 2007 exploits primacy: the reader learns the basis gap as a MEASURED QUANTITY before they ever see its consequence, so at 2007 they are recognizing, not inferring.

The stack ban is Cleveland & McGill directly. In a stacked area only the bottom band has a common baseline; every middle band is judged by length along a non-aligned scale, which is roughly twice the error of aligned position, and data-to-viz flags exactly this. With 27 medium labels that is fatal. The lane board converts every read back to aligned position (rank 1) at the cost of direct part-to-whole reading, which this data cannot honestly support anyway. Peak-year sorting adds a preattentive orientation cue — the diagonal — so the headline pattern arrives before any label is decoded. Rendering the 2011-2025 hole as a MATERIAL rather than as white space is the integrity move: blank canvas reads as zero, stipple reads as unmeasured.

hard_problems.solution:
Era 1 is not on the line. It is the bench the line is built on, and it gets a different physical register: SOUNDINGS.

The x-axis runs 1840-2026 always, but 1840-1918 carries no ribbon. It carries seven vertical plumb-lines at 1867, 1880, 1890, 1900, 1909, 1914, 1917 — each a full interval bar whose LENGTH is the 80% CI (1914: $990m-$1,450m, central $1,200m) with a small horizontal tick at the central. Between the soundings: nothing. Not interpolation, not a dotted guide, not a fade. Bone ground with the paper grid showing through.

Each sounding is a hollow outer bar with a SOLID INNER CORE: the grade-A Census of Manufactures receipts ($255.6m in 1914). Solid = what publishers actually received; hollow = a reconstruction of everything else, on a wider promotional-outlay basis of which print was only about 21%. One mark carries the entire era-1 measurement problem.

The reader's Gestalt instinct will be to connect the soundings, so the design pre-empts it. On first scroll into era 1, a ghost line SWEEPs through the seven centrals, holds 400ms, then dissolves, with one line: 'You can draw this line. Nobody has the data to.'

Narratively era 1 is not off the spine at all — it gets a full bench like every era, and its bench is where the reader learns the apparatus: Palmer's 25% publisher-paid commission at the TOLL, the 1875 open contract flipping the TOLL to the buyer's side, the classified counter at the GATE, and the 1914 founding of the Audit Bureau of Circulations lighting the METER for the first time.
hard_problems.cognitive_rationale:
Changing the MARK TYPE across the seam — bar versus ribbon — signals epistemic kind through preattentive shape, before a single label is read. This is Bertin's rule that the mark should declare what kind of thing it is, and it is far more reliable than a legend, because shape discrimination is parallel while legend lookup is serial and memory-loaded.

Drawing the ghost line and then removing it uses the GENERATION EFFECT: an error the reader produces themselves is retained better than a fact presented to them. It costs 1.3 seconds and inoculates against the single most likely misreading of the whole first act.

Empty space between soundings is not wasted data-ink; it is the inverse of Tufte's rule. Ink where there is no data is a lie. And the hollow-outer / solid-inner mark is a nested-extent encoding, which humans read accurately at two levels — enough to carry 'the trustworthy part is this much of the claimed part' without a second chart.

hard_problems.solution:
I adapt P1's measurement jitter rather than adopting it, and ration it hard. Three registers, chosen by WHAT KIND of uncertainty is present, plus a fourth for absence.

REGISTER 1 — WIDTH, for interval uncertainty on a continuous series. The ribbon's thickness IS the 80% CI. Grade A renders as a near-hairline; grade C as a fat translucent band. Static, so it survives print, screenshots and reduced-motion for free.

REGISTER 2 — TEXTURE, for source grade, redundantly coded with width. A: solid fill. B: 1px horizontal rule at 4px pitch. C: 45-degree hatch at 6px pitch. Three levels, discriminable at a glance, colorblind-safe, and hatch already means 'provisional' in engineering-drawing convention, so no legend has to be learned.

REGISTER 3 — TREMOR, reserved and scarce. Motion survives, but ONLY on the 65 claims whose 80% CI exceeds 60% of the central. Those are never drawn as points; they are drawn as tremor clouds whose position is genuinely unstable within the interval at ~1.2Hz, amplitude equal to the full CI in pixels, capped at 6px. A claim with a 5x interval visibly refuses to hold still.

This is enforced in code, not by guideline: the renderer computes ci_width/central, and above 0.6 drawPoint() throws and drawTremor() is called instead. The 65-claim rule becomes a build-time integrity guarantee.

REGISTER 4 — STIPPLE, for documented absence (ds-gap-001, and era 1's 37.8% unassigned residual).
hard_problems.cognitive_rationale:
Two reasons P1's approach does not transfer at P2's scale. First, motion and flicker are the strongest preattentive channels there are — which is exactly why they must be scarce. P1 had roughly 160 marks; P2's hero carries 1,573 points across eight series plus 505 claims. If everything shimmers, motion stops being a signal and becomes texture, and the pop-out that made it valuable is gone. Rationing it to 13% of claims keeps it a genuine singleton.

Second and more serious: on a TIME SERIES, jitter is a false statement. A jittering ribbon reads as 'the market wobbled', which mis-encodes epistemic uncertainty as data volatility. And most of P2's uncertainty is neither — a 23.4% basis gap is a systematic offset, not noise, and rendering it as tremor would be a category error. Width and texture are honest about systematic uncertainty in a way motion is not.

Width is used as a three-level CATEGORY signal (thin / medium / fat), not as a magnitude to be read off, which is the one job size does excellently. Texture is preattentive and survives every colorblindness type. The two together are redundantly coded, which is Ware's standard defence against any single-channel failure.

hard_problems.solution:
THE RECLASSIFIER — one block, two bins, and the total never moves.

The 2000 market is drawn as four bins of unit particles, one particle = $1B (247 particles on the Coen total), matching the standing object-constancy preference. Inside the local_retail bin sits a keyed sub-block with a marked outline: 11 particles = the $11,135m of LOCAL Yellow Pages money.

The control is a two-position rocker labelled with the RULE, never with the outcome. Position A: 'Split directories by WHO BOUGHT' (era-native, geographic). Position B: 'Put all directories in ONE intent pool' (cross-era comparable, unified-intent). Flip it and the 11 marked particles TRAVERSE from local_retail to direct_response in a 700ms arc, path faintly drawn for 200ms after arrival so the reader can verify where each unit went. Nothing else moves. The grand-total counter is pinned and visibly reads 247 both before and after.

Underneath runs the RANK STRIP: each pool's 80% interval as a horizontal bar on a shared share-of-market axis. In position A, local_retail [20.8, 33.0] and direct_response [19.0, 36.0] visibly overlap. Flip to B and local_retail's interval NARROWS to [20.8, 28.5] rather than translating — the ceiling falls by the whole block while the floor holds at 20.8, because 4.50 of the native 7.52 points of downside WAS the directory convention. Showing that asymmetric narrowing is the proof that the seam is a convention: settle the rule and what remains (3.02pp) is the dispersion the estimating lenses actually disagree about.

Above both positions, in Martian Mono and identical in both: 'UNRANKED EITHER WAY.' Verbatim constancy across the flip is the point. A 'SHOW THE ARITHMETIC' affordance prints 28.32 -> 23.82, 24.71 -> 29.21, 4.4995pp, cited to taxonomy_seam. The basis label itself CUTS rather than crossfades.
hard_problems.cognitive_rationale:
Presenting the two taxonomies as two static charts side by side forces a between-image comparison, which is the most expensive thing you can ask of a reader: each cross-saccade comparison costs roughly one item of visual working memory, and the reader's conclusion will be shape-based — 'the market looks different under the two views' — which is precisely the false inference.

Animating the transition with preserved object identity converts a MEMORY comparison into a PERCEPTUAL one. The reader does not infer conservation; they watch it. Eleven identifiable objects walk from one bin to another and the total counter refuses to move. That is a causal-perception result — the visual system attributes conservation automatically when identity is preserved through motion — and it delivers the argument with no prose at all.

Labelling the rocker by RULE rather than by OUTCOME is a framing guard. A control labelled 'local retail leads / direct response leads' would invite the reader to choose a fact. A control labelled with two classification rules invites them to choose a convention, which is what is actually on offer.

And the invariant readout is the anti-anchoring device. If the verdict text changed with the toggle, the reader would anchor on whichever they saw first. Holding four words identical across the flip is the strongest available statement that the flip decides nothing.

hard_problems.solution:
THE UNRANKED FLOAT. Do not give the three unranked pools a positional order, in either axis.

One horizontal axis: share of the US market, 0-50%. Classified sits ALONE in its own region below a rule, labelled 'the only ordering the evidence supports' — its interval [1.4, 6.8] does not touch any other bar, and being separated by a rule is what encodes that it IS ranked (Gestalt common region doing the ordinal work that position would otherwise do).

The other three — national_brand, local_retail, direct_response — share one region above the rule, drawn on the same baseline as three overlapping translucent interval bars with NO vertical axis, NO ordinal labels, and no sort. Their vertical order within the region is randomized at render and re-shuffles on a slow 4s cycle, one swap at a time, when the section is in view. The visual refuses to commit, and the reader can watch it refusing.

The resting state (and the reduced-motion state, and the state the shuffle settles into after three cycles) is static: three bars in the shared region, direct-labelled at their centrals, with the overlap region between them filled with a distinct crosshatch and one caption: 'These three overlap. No order is established.' Readout beneath: national brand and direct response centrals sit 1.4 points apart on intervals about 18-20 points wide.

Enforced in code the same way as P3: renderPools() takes ordering: 'established' | 'unranked' and THROWS on 'unranked' if asked for a stack, a bar chart or a sorted list.
hard_problems.cognitive_rationale:
Position along a common scale is Cleveland & McGill rank 1 — the most accurate encoding available — which is exactly why it is the wrong one here. A rank-1 encoding will be BELIEVED. When the evidence cannot support an ordering, the correct move is to deliberately step DOWN the encoding hierarchy to a channel that cannot assert order. Overlapping translucent extents on a shared baseline encode magnitude-with-uncertainty while encoding no ordinal relation at all.

Stacking would be worse still: a stack asserts both an order AND a part-to-whole partition, two claims for the price of one, neither supported.

Separating classified into its own common region is the load-bearing detail. If all four sat together, the reader would read the whole exhibit as 'nothing is known,' which understates the record — classified's ranking IS established at 0.97 confidence. Two regions say two different epistemic things with one boundary line.

The deliberate instability re-uses the tremor grammar from P3 one level up: the mark trembles when the value is uncertain, the LAYOUT trembles when the ORDER is uncertain. Same idea, same reading, no new vocabulary.

hard_problems.solution:
THE AUCTION BENCH — the era-6 bench with its RULE organ opened up. Not a special widget; the same apparatus with five knobs instead of one. Fixed layout: LEFT the cast (Aster Auto Cover, Brindle Brokers, Cedar Cover, persistent across all scenarios, each marked 'INVENTED — teaches the mechanism, does not measure Google's book'). CENTRE the page, two slots. RIGHT the TILL — three readouts that never move: REVENUE / 1000 SHOWINGS, CLICKS, AVG PRICE PER CLICK. BOTTOM the rule strip: RANK BY, PRICE AT, RESERVE, gamma, FORMAT, BIDDER MODE.

sc-01 -> sc-02 as one motion: the reader flips RANK BY and the three ads physically swap slots (object constancy). Till: $28.18 -> $52.58, 18 -> 58 clicks, $1.57 -> $0.91. Revenue and price needles are animated moving in OPPOSITE directions, with one caption: 'The seller earned 87% more and charged 42% less.'

sc-03: per-winner bid-vs-price drop brackets, plus the pay-your-bid row tagged FROZEN BIDS — NOT A FORECAST.

sc-04: control changes hands. The reader drags one bidder's own bid; the Till's top readout re-labels to YOUR PAYOFF and the seller's revenue greys out. $400 truthful -> $640 shaded. Perspective switches by relabelling a fixed readout, never by moving to a new screen.

sc-05 THE BAND — the signature. From here on, REVENUE is not a number: it is a marker inside a drawn track from $440 (lowest envy-free) to $760 (naive truthful). The three-position toggle moves it. And every revenue figure elsewhere in the simulator thereafter carries the toggle's current position as a label, exactly as the data file specifies.

sc-06: two bars, n in {2,3,5,10}, shading slider starting AT (n-1)/n so the bars begin LEVEL and the reader breaks equivalence rather than discovering it. Permanent chip: 'This was display. Search never went to first price.' And the frozen-bid trap shown explicitly: the apparent 86% windfall exists only if nobody re-bids.

sc-07: one slider on Cedar's TRUE click rate; the PREDICTED value pinned in a physically detached box marked SELLER'S OWN FORECAST — NOT AUDITED UNTIL 2009. Break-even ticked at 1.99%.

sc-08: one slot, one bidder, reserve 1c -> $1.00, revenue $0.40 -> $40. The page above is pinned and a chip stays lit: USER EXPERIENCE: UNCHANGED.

sc-09: gamma, format and rGSP on the same cast. gamma=0.5 restores the pure-bid allocation (18 clicks, not 58) while collecting 45% more than pure bid ever did. Assumed and disclosed parameters get DIFFERENT CHIP COLOURS: 'gamma IS ASSUMED — named in the court record, exponent never disclosed' versus 'DISCLOSED + citation'.

sc-10: 2019, two panels, arrows opposite. Display first-price: revenue change 0.0. Search rGSP: +5.74% — which moves the market 7.9% of the way across a band the mechanism leaves 73% wide.

DEAD-MECHANISM GUARD, by constraint rather than warning: on the search bench, PRICE AT = first is RAIL-LOCKED. The control greys and cannot be set. You cannot mis-teach what the interface will not let you do.
hard_problems.cognitive_rationale:
The three-readout Till is a fixed instrument panel, so every scenario is read as a DELTA on a stable frame rather than as a fresh picture. That is what makes 21 scenarios one experience: change blindness is defeated by holding everything constant except the one thing under test, which is also the scrollytelling rule of one change at a time.

The CRANK verb's 40ms hold between input and output is deliberate. Zero lag reads as rendering; a short, consistent lag reads as MECHANISM, because the visual system attributes causality to temporally offset event pairs. This is Mayer's temporal-contiguity principle applied to interaction, and it is the single cheapest thing that makes the machine feel operated rather than animated.

Starting sc-06's shading slider AT equilibrium is an anchoring decision. Whatever the reader sees first becomes the reference. Showing equivalence first and deviation second means the anchor is the true claim; the reverse ordering would teach that first-price is a windfall, which is the exact error the frozen-bid trap documents.

And THE BAND does the deepest work: it retro-actively converts every revenue number in the piece from a fact into a position. Once the reader has personally dragged the seller's revenue by 73% with the mechanism, the bidders and the query all frozen, the +5.74% rGSP uplift can never be read as 'the seller set the price'. That reframing is impossible to achieve with prose and trivial with a track and a marker.

hard_problems.solution:
The eight-field schema is a FLOOR PLAN, not a table. Eight organs at eight fixed screen positions, identical in all seven benches: INLET (buyers), GATE (entry terms), METER (measurement), RULE (pricing), SORTER (targeting), DOOR (front-door owner), TOLL (intermediary cut), OUTLET (sellers), with SCALE as a dial and EVENTS as a strip beneath.

Cross-era comparison is THE ORGAN PULL. Every organ label is a control. Click PRICING on era 3's bench and the page does NOT navigate — a strip slides up from the bottom edge showing that one organ from all seven benches side by side in era order, at small scale, with era 3's instance highlighted in place. Release and it slides back. Scroll position is never lost. That answers 'compare era 3's pricing to era 6's without scrolling twice' literally: no scrolling at all — the comparison comes to the reader.

The four thread chapters are the organ pull made permanent and full-screen. So the reader learns the gesture in chapter 2 and the thread chapters are the same gesture at full size, with room for annotation. No new form to learn at the moment the material gets hardest.

The full 56-cell matrix also exists as one static reference page: a 7x8 grid, era rows by organ columns, each cell a ~90x54px glyph plus a four-to-six-word label. It is linked from every bench and from every thread chapter. Rows read as eras; columns read as threads; the four selected threads' columns are tinted.
hard_problems.cognitive_rationale:
Fixed spatial position converts recall into recognition, which is the single largest cognitive saving available in a long-form piece. Norman's knowledge-in-the-world argument, applied at chapter scale: the reader never has to remember where pricing lives, because pricing is always in the same place, and after two benches that position is encoded spatially rather than verbally.

The organ pull respects the fact that scroll-position loss is the dominant cost in scrollytelling. A modal or a jump-link forces re-orientation on return, which throws away the narrative context the reader has just built. A peek strip costs nothing, which is Shneiderman's details-on-demand with the crucial added constraint of spatial persistence.

The 56-cell grid is never asked to be READ — 56 items is ten times working memory and reading it linearly would be miserable. It is asked to be SCANNED for pattern, which is a preattentive task provided the glyph vocabulary is consistent across all 56 cells. Row-scan and column-scan then give two different findings from one artefact, which is exactly the Gestalt continuity payoff of a strict grid.

hard_problems.solution:
The honest position, stated in the build brief: on mobile the reader is SHOWN the mechanism; on desktop the reader OPERATES it. I will not pretend the two are equal.

STICKY HERO -> CARD DECK. Below 768px the hero un-sticks entirely. Each scene becomes a full-width non-sticky card: chart above, ~40 words below, one scene per swipe-height. A sticky chart on a 667px-tall phone leaves about 220px for prose, which fails the reading experience harder than any type choice could.

SIMULATOR -> THE STEPPER. The scenarios collapse to nine pre-computed states (sc-01 through sc-09) as a horizontally swipeable stack. Nothing is solved on device — every state renders from expected_output in simulator-params.json. Each state gets exactly ONE live control, always in the same place (bottom third, thumb zone, 44px minimum target): sc-02 gets the RANK BY rocker, sc-05 gets the three-position band toggle, sc-08 gets the reserve rocker. Everything else is a stepped preset with a caption.

LANE BOARD -> TIME RUNS DOWN. On mobile the lane board rotates so time flows vertically, matching the scroll gesture, with 5-6 lanes visible in a horizontally scrollable group and the era markers pinned.

DELIBERATELY DROPPED, and named in the spec so nobody quietly re-adds them: (a) free-form sliders — every slider becomes a two- or three-position rocker using the marked_stops already in the data file; (b) simultaneous multi-knob exploration — sc-09's three knobs become three sequential single-knob cards, and the stacked 1.1036 result is STATED rather than discovered; (c) the organ-pull peek strip — replaced by a link to the 56-cell grid, rendered on mobile as a per-era vertical list; (d) hover tooltips entirely — every value that would be a tooltip is either printed on the mark or reachable by tap-to-pin; (e) TREMOR — off by default below 768px for battery and small-mark legibility, with the static hatched-interval form as the default and a 'show the shimmer' toggle in the reading-settings sheet.
hard_problems.cognitive_rationale:
A sticky hero works because it holds the visual referent in view while prose changes, removing the need to re-acquire it. That trade only pays when the remaining prose column is large enough to read comfortably. Below roughly 768px it inverts: the reader pays the cost of a shrunken chart AND a cramped column, and gets neither.

Rockers instead of sliders is a Fitts's law and precision argument. A continuous slider on a touch screen has an effective resolution of maybe 40 discrete positions under a thumb, most of which are meaningless, and the reader must both aim and interpret. A three-position rocker with stops taken from the data file's own marked_stops removes the aiming problem entirely and guarantees the reader lands on a value the research actually supports.

Dropping multi-knob exploration is the honest one. Discovering an interaction effect requires holding two changes in working memory at once while manipulating a third — that is genuinely over budget on a phone, and pretending otherwise produces a reader who taps randomly and learns nothing. Stating the stacked result and letting the reader verify each knob singly preserves the finding and drops only the discovery.

hard_problems.solution:
THREAD 1 — THE METER STRIP. I accept the two-track timeline and argue for one change: do not encode the funder as seven categorical colours. Encode it as VERTICAL DEPTH BELOW THE AXIS, ordered by distance from the seller — 'nobody' deepest, then industry (three-sided), advertiser, rival medium, vendor, publisher, and 'seller' flush against the axis at depth zero. Colour is retained but demoted to a redundant sequential ramp. The thread then reads as one geometric fact: from 1914 to about 1996 the funder blocks hang deep below the axis; after 1996 they rise and COLLAPSE onto it. The two natural experiments are the interactive beats. 1987: an inline DIARY | PEOPLE METER two-state at that x-position — flip it and measured prime-time audience falls 10%, CBS -13%, ABC -13%, with nothing else changed. Label: 'Same viewing. Two instruments. Two prices.' 2021: a second flip for the Nielsen 2-6% undercount, valued at $468M+ of lost national ad revenue, drawn as a dollar bar against that year's total.

THREAD 2 — THE TOLL STACK. Seven vertical bars, 'where each advertiser dollar goes', under a declared convention stated in a fixed caption. Era 1 is a clean 15% agency block on 85% publisher. Era 7's bar CANNOT BE CLOSED: known blocks build from the bottom and the top is an open, hatched, RAGGED-EDGED block labelled 'UNKNOWN — the ISBA study could not trace it.' All seven drawn at once, so the eye lands on the one that doesn't close. Honesty guard, because the denominators genuinely differ (% of gross billings / % of net time sales retained / gross margin / % of network revenue / % of an end-to-end chain): each bar carries its own denominator chip in Plex Mono, hover dims the rest and prints that bar's base full-width, and a permanent line reads 'These are not one quantity. Each bar names its own base.'

THREAD 3 — TWO PANELS THAT MUST NOT BE JOINED. A 48px gutter of bare paper (proximity, not a divider line). Left, eras 1-4: the classified and directory DOLLAR SHARE, stubbornly 3-13%, in lane-board grammar. Right, eras 5-7: the advertiser HEAD COUNT, 3,800 -> 53,000 -> 80,000 -> ~1M -> >10M on a log axis, with grade-C intervals as genuinely large bands (Google's is 550k-2.6M, a 4.7x band, drawn at its true width). The gutter carries one line: 'Left is money. Right is bodies. They are not one line.' Between them, THE GATE CARD: the A-grade Overture-versus-AdWords side-by-side in the same year, four rows — deposit, monthly minimum, review, approval time — drawn as two literal gates, one with a queue and one standing open. This is the cleanest causal exhibit in the record and it gets the plainest treatment on the page.

THREAD 4 — ONE INSTRUMENT, SEVEN INSTANCES, TWO AXES. Seven small panels showing the front-door payout as a SHARE of the revenue it generated (~27% radio affiliate comp -> 56% -> 85% AOL -> ~36%), so the rates are comparable. Beneath all seven, one continuous absolute-dollar strip on which $26.3B in 2021 — 57.7% of all traffic acquisition cost — simply swamps everything before it. The two-axis design IS the finding: the rate barely moved in 80 years while the base moved four orders of magnitude. Inset: the AOL warrant, cost at signature ($13.871M carrying value, $21.6M total exercise price for 7,437,452 shares) against cost realised (~$1.135B), two bars 82x apart, captioned 'Distribution paid in equity looks cheap when you sign it.' The strip then continues UNINTERRUPTED past the September 2025 remedy line.
hard_problems.cognitive_rationale:
The thread-1 change is the important argument. Seven categorical colours exceeds the reliable limit for categorical colour identification, and worse, it forces a serial legend lookup for every block — the reader must decode each one before the pattern can emerge. But those seven categories have a meaningful ORDER: distance from the seller. Mapping an ordered variable to a nominal channel throws away the structure. Re-mapping it to depth converts the whole thread from a lookup task to a length-and-position judgment, which is parallel and Cleveland & McGill rank 1. The finding — independence collapsed after 1996 — then arrives as a SHAPE, before any label is read. That is what a grade-A thread deserves.

Thread 2's incompleteness is a shape singleton: six closed bars and one open one is a preattentive pop-out, so the finding lands before the caption. And the denominator chips are the fallacy guard — seven bars in a row is a powerful invitation to read them as one series, which they are not.

Thread 3's gutter uses proximity rather than a rule, because a divider line is still a connector; bare ground is the strongest possible statement of non-relation. Drawing the 4.7x interval at its true width rather than a token width is the integrity requirement — a wide interval drawn narrow is a lie about confidence.

Thread 4's dual axis is normally a fallacy pattern, and it is safe here only because the two axes are STACKED as separate panels rather than overlaid on one plot. Overlaying would invite a spurious correlation reading between rate and base. Stacking asks the reader to compare two independent facts about the same instrument, which is exactly the claim.

proposals.type:
Four faces, each with exactly one job, and the jobs never overlap.

MARTIAN MONO (variable, subset, preloaded) — every numeral and every readout. The Till's three values, all 80% intervals, all era years, the grade counts. Tabular figures are non-negotiable here: in the simulator a readout updates at frame rate during a drag, and proportional digits would make the number physically jitter, which would collide with TREMOR's meaning. KEPT from P1.

NEWSREADER (variable, subset, preloaded) — body prose only. 19px/1.65 desktop, 17px/1.6 mobile, max 62ch, ink at 100% for primary and 80% for secondary. This face is a DEFENSIVE requirement: a page of iron line-work and monospace readouts reads cold and hostile without a warm serif carrying the argument. KEPT from P1.

IBM PLEX MONO — data chrome. Tooltips, CI values, A/B/C grade marks, denominator chips, source citations, the 'SHOW THE ARITHMETIC' panels. 12-13px. KEPT from P1.

INSTRUMENT SANS (fallback: Inter Tight) — NEW, and restricted to ARCHITECTURE labels only: the eight organ names (INLET, GATE, METER, RULE, SORTER, DOOR, TOLL, OUTLET), every knob label, every panel title. Uppercase, +0.08em tracking, 11-12px, zinc. The reason it exists rather than reusing Plex Mono: organ labels are structure, not data, and if a knob label can be mistaken for a value the whole bench grammar fails. A small-caps grotesque removes that ambiguity at zero reading cost. Four faces is the ceiling; if the combined review wants three, this is the one to cut, and organ labels move to Plex Mono at 500 weight with wider tracking.

Grade marks are rendered as typographic objects in Plex Mono with their P3 textures applied — A solid, B ruled, C hatched — so the letter and the texture always travel together and the reader learns the mapping from the first screen.
proposals.motion:
SIX NAMED VERBS.

SETTLE — 700ms, cubic-bezier(.16,1,.3,1). Critically damped arrival. Any value reaching its measured position: particle landings, slot snaps, readout arrivals. KEPT from P1.

SWEEP — near-linear, cubic-bezier(.4,0,.6,1), ~1400ms across the viewport. Time-axis draws, left to right, chart-recorder pen. All rails and lanes draw with SWEEP. KEPT from P1.

CRANK — NEW, and the signature verb. 320ms, cubic-bezier(.34,0,.2,1), with a deliberate 40ms HOLD before the output moves. Every rule change uses it: the machine takes the input, pauses a beat, then the output responds. The hold is load-bearing — it separates cause from effect in time so the reader attributes the change to their own hand.

TRAVERSE — 700ms SETTLE along an arc, for object-constancy particle moves (P4's eleven Yellow Pages units, the simulator's slot swaps). The path is drawn faintly for 200ms after arrival, then fades, so the reader can verify where each unit went. This is the object-constancy guarantee made visible rather than merely asserted.

TREMOR — continuous ~1.2Hz, amplitude = the full 80% CI in pixels, capped at 6px. ONLY on the 65 claims where ci_width/central > 0.6. Never on ribbons, never on totals, never on era spines.

CUT — 0ms. No transition at all. Reserved for exactly one thing: crossing a definitional seam. Switching basis label from Coen to Magna, or flipping the era-5 taxonomy label, CUTS. A crossfade would imply continuity between two things that are not continuous, and transitions imply relatedness — so where there is no relation there must be no transition.

Particles snap; they never float, drift or bounce. Scene changes are scroll-driven, one change at a time — highlight OR annotate, never both. No parallax. No scroll-jacking, ever.

PREFERS-REDUCED-MOTION: REDUCE — the complete fallback.
- TREMOR becomes a static hollow lozenge with a hatched interior, both interval endpoints ticked, and the interval printed in Plex Mono. It is NEVER rendered as a point, in any mode. That is a data-integrity rule, not a motion preference.
- SETTLE and TRAVERSE become a 120ms crossfade PLUS a persistent origin ghost: the particle's previous position stays drawn at 25% opacity for 3 seconds. This is essential — P4's conservation proof is motion-carried, so the fallback must carry it another way, and the ghost lets the reader still see that the same eleven units moved and the total did not change.
- SWEEP renders complete in one frame.
- CRANK's 40ms hold becomes a 200ms two-step HIGHLIGHT: input flashes, then output flashes. Sequence preserved, motion removed.
- CUT is unchanged; it was already zero.
- P5's unranked shuffle stops entirely and renders the static overlap-crosshatch form with its caption.
- The simulator remains fully operable; only the transitions between states are removed.
proposals.signature_interaction:
THE BAND. In the auction bench, from sc-05 onward, the REVENUE readout stops being a number. It becomes a marker inside a drawn track running from $440 (the lowest envy-free equilibrium) to $760 (naive truthful bidding). A three-position toggle — naive truthful / one shader / lowest envy-free — moves the marker. The mechanism does not change. The bidders do not change. The query does not change. The reader's own hand moves the seller's revenue by 73%.

The line that lands: "Same rule. Same bidders. The price is whatever they let it be."

Then the rule that makes everything downstream honest, and which the data file itself specifies: once the band exists, EVERY revenue figure elsewhere in the simulator carries the toggle's current position as a label. So when the reader reaches rGSP's disclosed +5.74% uplift, they do not see a price increase. They see a tiny nudge — 7.9% of the way — across a band they personally dragged five minutes earlier, a band the mechanism itself leaves 73% wide.

This is the interaction the reader remembers because it retro-actively rewrites everything they thought they had learned. They arrived believing the auction sets the price. They leave knowing the auction under-determines the price, and that the seller sits on the band. That is chapter 7's real finding, it cannot be delivered by prose, and it is the argument the whole capture question in chapter 9 rests on.

(Runner-up, and the one that best serves the threads: THE RECLASSIFIER — eleven brass particles walking from one bin to another while the grand total counter visibly refuses to move.)
proposals.what_it_sacrifices:
1. FRONT-LOADED LEARNING COST. The bench grammar must be taught before it pays anything back. Chapter 2 spends roughly 90 seconds of reader attention teaching a diagram. Readers who bounce in chapter 2 get strictly less than they would from a plain annotated-chart direction, which is legible in three seconds. This is the direction's largest and least fixable risk.

2. IT IS WORSE AT THE SWEEP OF THE CENTURY. The most emotionally available thing in this material is "here is 180 years on one screen." My chart system deliberately refuses to draw that as one line — three rails, calipers, soundings, stipple, a ragged cut edge. A reader who wants the FEELING of a century gets less of it than from a direction that draws the honest-but-spliced line with a prominent warning. I am trading emotional legibility for evidentiary honesty and that is a real loss, not a clever win.

3. THE MECHANISM FRAME IS COLD FOR A STORY ABOUT POWER. The patent-medicine trust crisis, the 91% collapse in help-wanted classified, the shopkeeper who could suddenly buy a national medium — these are people, and a bench diagram flattens them into inputs and outputs. A direction built on the INSTITUTIONS frame (a court, a cartel, the room where the rate is set) would carry the four threads' politics better than mine does. Naming the organs after power relations is a mitigation, not a solution.

4. FOUR TYPEFACES AND EIGHT NAMED COLOURS IS A LOT OF SYSTEM. Every item is individually defensible and the aggregate is heavy. A stricter direction ships three faces and five colours and stays consistent across ten chapters more easily than this will.

5. THE P5 UNRANKED SHUFFLE IS GENUINELY RISKY. A visual that deliberately refuses to hold still can read as broken, and some readers will report it as a bug rather than as a claim. I believe it is right and I have shipped a static fallback, but I would want it tested, and if five readers in a row call it broken I would not fight to keep it.

6. DESKTOP-FAVOURED BY DESIGN. Mobile drops free-form sliders, multi-knob exploration, the organ pull, and hover entirely. On mobile this is a demonstration; on desktop it is an instrument. A mobile-native, card-first direction would be more equal across devices and less capable on both — I chose capability over equality, and phone readers pay for it.

7. SEVEN BENCHES IS STILL SEVEN BENCHES. Even amortized, the interaction budget is the biggest structural gamble here. If the era 3, 4 and 5 cranks are not genuinely satisfying inside about 30 seconds each, the reader arrives at era 6 depleted rather than fluent, and the auction simulator inherits a tired audience instead of a trained one. The whole argument for the direction rests on those three middle cranks being good, and they are the least glamorous things to build.
